title: Remember this
summary: Use memory cells to store values, change them, and retrieve them later.

scenario.briefing: The pickup desk stores an order code and a box count. The clerk needs the shelf label to read A7 and the count to reach 3 before the next step can run.

objectives.description: Store the required values in memory.
Predict the value after an assignment.
Check understanding through the remaining explanation and transfer evidence.

hints: Each operation changes one or both cells. Watch the cells after every click.
Set the code directly, then set the count and add one.
You need pickupCode A7 and boxCount 3. Set the count to 2, then use the operation that adds one.
Run: store A7, set boxCount to 2, add 1 to boxCount.

misconceptions.description: Treating assignment as a permanent mathematical equality.
misconceptions.feedback: Assignment stores the current value. A later assignment can replace it. The cell is not locked to that number forever.

misconceptions.description: Applying an add before the set that should follow it.
misconceptions.diagnostic: Applies add-one before set-two, so the later set overwrites the increment and boxCount ends at 2 instead of 3.
misconceptions.feedback: The last write wins. If set-two runs after add-one, the increment is lost. Order the writes so the desired value is written last.

misconceptions.description: Believing stored values cannot affect later output.
misconceptions.feedback: Stored values are exactly what later steps read. A total, cart, or pickup code changes the output of the steps that follow.

sections.title: State is remembered information
sections.body: A memory cell holds a value that later instructions can read or replace. The pickup code and box count are state. Without state, every instruction would start from nothing.

sections.title: Assignment changes state
sections.body: The operation set boxCount to 2 stores 2. Add one reads the current value, computes 3, and stores the result back. Assignment is not the same as mathematical equality: a later step can assign a different value.

vocabulary.definition: Values a system remembers between steps.
Storing a value into a named cell.
Reading a stored value for later use.

hints: Apply operations until both memory cells match the target state.
State changes only when an operation writes to a cell, and a later write replaces an earlier one.
To reach 3 from 0 you can set 2 and then add 1, but only when the add happens after the set.
Set the pickup code first, then reach a box count of 3 with two writes in the right order.
steps.title: Set the pickup desk memory
steps.prompt: Apply operations until the memory matches the target. Operations may be applied in a useful order; each click changes state.
steps.explanation: The final state holds A7 and 3. The operations changed memory one step at a time.

steps.title: What remains after assignment?
steps.prompt: A program runs: bagCount = 2, then bagCount = 5. What does bagCount hold afterwards?

quiz.prompt: Choose the value after both assignments.
quiz.explanation: The second assignment replaces the stored value. The cell holds 5 after the program reaches that line.

hints: Track the stored value after each of the two assignment lines.
Assignment replaces the current value; it does not create a permanent equation.
If x = 1 and then x = 9, x holds 9 afterward, not both values.
The second line runs after the first. Decide which write the cell keeps, then choose that value.
Select claims that describe how stored values behave across steps.
State carries results forward and can be overwritten by later steps.
A shopping cart total that persists between clicks depends on stored state.
Two statements are true; reject the claims that state is invisible or that different state must behave identically.
steps.title: State and correctness
steps.prompt: Select the accurate statements about state.

statements.label: State lets later steps reuse earlier results.
A later assignment can replace an earlier value.
Two programs with different state must behave identically.

steps.explanation: State carries information forward and can change. Two systems starting from different state can produce different output.

accessibility.summary: Each memory cell is exposed as a labeled value. Operations are normal buttons and the target is always visible as text.
accessibility.keyboardNotes: Tab to an operation and press Enter or Space. The updated cells are announced politely.
accessibility.screenReaderNotes: The target reads pickupCode A7 and boxCount 3. Cell changes are announced after every operation.
